questions.question: Using the line segment formula, how many segments do 6 points on a line form?
Using the line segment formula, how many segments do 7 points on a line form?
Why does the lesson warn that 'memorization can fail' for advanced triangle counting formulas?
options: Formulas always work regardless of the figure
Because complex or irregular figures often don't match the exact conditions a memorized formula assumes, leading to a wrong answer if applied blindly
Because triangle formulas don't actually exist
Because memorization is always faster than understanding
questions.rationale: A memorized formula only applies correctly when a figure matches its underlying assumptions — applying it blindly to an irregular or non-matching figure produces a wrong answer.

questions.question: What is the recommended 'best strategy for exam' figure-counting questions, according to this lesson?
options: Always guess a round number
Skip figure-counting questions entirely
Only ever use manual counting, never formulas
Apply a known formula when the figure is regular, but fall back to a systematic manual counting method (checklist, labeling) when it isn't
questions.rationale: The recommended strategy is flexible: use a direct formula for regular, formula-matching figures, but rely on the systematic manual method for irregular ones.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a '30-second verification' step after arriving at a count?
options: A quick sanity check (like re-counting a subset or checking against a known formula) to catch an obviously wrong answer before finalizing it
To waste time before submitting
To redraw the entire figure
To convert the answer into a different unit
questions.rationale: A brief verification step — like spot-checking a subset of the count or comparing against a known formula — helps catch an obviously wrong answer before it's finalized.

questions.question: What does the 'final universal algorithm' aim to consolidate?
options: Only the formulas for triangles
A single formula that replaces all others
The full set of counting steps and checks covered throughout the lesson into one repeatable procedure applicable to any figure-counting problem
Only the practice examples, not the theory
questions.rationale: The final universal algorithm brings together every step and check covered throughout the lesson into one repeatable, general-purpose counting procedure.

questions.question: Why are 'common exam question types' highlighted separately in this lesson?
options: They aren't actually relevant to exams
To help recognize which specific method or formula is likely to apply based on the style of question typically seen in exams
To discourage practicing with real exam questions
Because exam questions never repeat any pattern
questions.rationale: Highlighting common question types helps a learner quickly recognize which method or formula is likely to apply, based on patterns seen in typical exam questions.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a 'figure counting master table'?
options: To replace all previous explanations
To consolidate the various formulas (segments, squares, rectangles, intersections, regions) into one single quick-reference summary
To only list answers with no formulas
To discourage using formulas during practice
questions.rationale: A master table brings together every formula covered — segments, squares, rectangles, intersections, regions — into one consolidated, easy-to-scan reference.

questions.question: Using the line segment formula, how many points on a line are needed to form exactly 21 segments?
questions.rationale: Since n(n-1)/2 = 21 gives n = 7 (7 x 6 / 2 = 21), 7 points are needed.

questions.question: What is the general benefit of having formula charts (segment, intersection, region) available together, rather than scattered across the lesson?
options: There is no real benefit
It allows quick lookup and comparison during practice or exam review without needing to re-derive each formula from scratch
It makes the formulas less accurate
It only helps with segment formulas, not the others
questions.rationale: Consolidated formula charts allow fast lookup and comparison during practice or review, saving the time of re-deriving each formula individually from first principles.
